THOUGHT: This 27-year-old unrestrained male sustained a high-impact head-on motor vehicle collision and now presents with chest pain, chest wall bruising, tachycardia (HR 120), hypotension (BP 107/58), and elevated troponins. Although chest X-ray shows no rib fractures or pneumothorax, and echocardiogram shows normal chamber sizes and valves, the combination of traumatic mechanism, chest wall contusion, sinus tachycardia, hypotension, elevated troponin, and—critically—elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is highly suggestive of myocardial injury due to blunt cardiac trauma. Elevated PCWP indicates increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, consistent with impaired left ventricular compliance or systolic/diastolic dysfunction — not explained by isolated chest wall injury. Normal echocardiogram does not rule out myocardial contusion, as wall motion abnormalities may be subtle, transient, or regional and missed on standard views; troponin elevation confirms myocardial cell injury. Other diagnoses (e.g., aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade) are unlikely: no widened mediastinum on CXR, no muffled heart sounds or JVD or pulsus paradoxus on exam, no respiratory distress or asymmetric breath sounds, and echo shows no pericardial effusion or RV collapse. Pulmonary contusion is possible but would not explain elevated PCWP or troponin. Thus, the most coherent unifying diagnosis is blunt myocardial injury — specifically myocardial contusion — given the mechanism, clinical presentation, biomarker elevation, hemodynamic findings (elevated PCWP + tachycardia + borderline hypotension), and absence of alternative structural explanations.

DIAGNOSIS: Myocardial contusion
